title: Harvesting pea shoots
subtitle: When and how to cut, rinse, and store pea shoots at peak quality
excerpt: Pea shoots are ready to harvest when the first curling tendrils appear and the shoots are 8 to 12 cm tall, around day 10 to 14. Cut 2 to 3 cm above the medium (higher than for brassicas, to get the tender tip without the coarser base). Pea shoots often produce a second cut.
sourceNotes: UMass Extension microgreens guides (open-access). Cornell Cooperative Extension indoor growing material. Standard microgreen-growing practice synthesised from extension service material.

glossaryTerms.definition: The curling, thread-like extension that appears on pea shoots as the plant develops. In mature pea plants, tendrils attach to supports and hold the plant upright. In pea microgreens, the first tendrils signal that the shoot is at peak quality for harvesting — tender, sweet, and with the best combination of leaf and stem texture.

A second harvest from the same tray of microgreens after the first cut, from the regrowth that emerges from the remaining root-and-stem stub. Most microgreen crops do not regrow usefully after the first cut. Pea shoots are one of the exceptions: the roots store enough energy to produce a second crop of shorter, slightly coarser shoots within 7 to 10 days.

content.text: Pea shoots are one of the most rewarding microgreens to harvest: the shoots are substantial, fragrant, and often yield a second crop from the same tray. Timing is easy to judge; the first curling tendrils are the sign the shoots are ready.

are the timing signal: when the first curling thread-like extensions appear and the shoots are 8 to 12 cm tall, the tray is ready. At this stage the upper leaves are tender and sweet; the base of the stem is slightly tougher. Cut before the upper leaves fully unfold into mature leaflets.

The window for pea shoots is somewhat longer than for brassica cotyledons: several days rather than 24 to 48 hours. But quality declines if the stems become fibrous at the base; don't leave too long after the first tendrils appear.

Use clean scissors. Cut 2 to 3 cm above the medium surface, higher than for most brassica microgreens. This higher cut leaves behind the toughest part of the stem while capturing the tender upper shoot and the developing tendrils.
Work across the tray in one pass, cutting even rows. Pea shoots are large enough that cutting in sections and gathering as you go is easiest.

: after the first harvest, leave the tray in a bright position and continue bottom-watering. Within 7 to 10 days, new shoots emerge from the cut stubs. The second cut produces shorter shoots of slightly coarser texture. Most growers find the first cut produces the best quality; the second cut is a bonus crop, not a replacement for a fresh tray.

Rinse cut pea shoots under cold running water. Shake out excess moisture. Pea shoots store better than most microgreens: refrigerate in a sealed container for up to two days. The larger shoot structure holds up better than brassica cotyledons.

attrs.heading: Troubleshooting
attrs.intro: Common harvest-stage problems with pea shoots.

items.symptom: Shoots lean strongly to one side when cut
items.cause: Single-direction light source not balanced by daily tray rotation.
items.fix: Rotate the tray 180 degrees every day during the light phase on the next batch. A grow light directly above the tray eliminates this entirely.

items.symptom: Base of stems tough and fibrous
items.cause: Harvested after the stems have lignified.
items.fix: Cut as soon as the first tendrils appear and before the leaves fully unfold. Alternatively, cut higher (3 cm from the medium) on the next batch to ensure only the tender upper shoot is captured.

items.symptom: No regrowth for a second cut after 10 days
items.cause: Root energy reserves depleted or cut too low.
items.fix: Some trays don't produce a meaningful second crop; start a fresh tray instead. Cut a little higher on the next first cut (leave 3 to 4 cm stub) to leave more energy for regrowth.
